question: to the Commission Dick Erixon (ECR) Subject:

The Commission has urged Member States to accelerate the deployment of online age verification tools. At the Commission press conference on 29 April 2026, a question was raised about whether minors could use VPN services to circumvent such tools. In reply, Commission Executive Vice-President Henna Virkkunen stated that it is difficult to make any technological solution impossible to circumvent. She added that the Commission must ensure the implementation of the rules and will look at preventing circumvention, in particular for high-risk services. VPN services are widely used by businesses, public authorities, journalists, lawyers, doctors and private individuals, including minors, to enhance cybersecurity and privacy when using public Wi-Fi networks. Any EU-level restriction, ban or age limit on VPN services could therefore have significant implications for privacy, security and freedom of communication. 1.
Can the Commission confirm whether any EU-wide ban, restriction, age limit or identification requirement for VPN services is currently being discussed, assessed or prepared?
If such measures are being considered, what is their legal basis?
What safeguards are proposed to protect freedom of communication?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (29.6.2026) The Commission’s work on the protection of minors is grounded in a comprehensive, ambitious, and rights-based EU framework1, which combines strong legislative measures, such as the Digital Services Act2, and rigorous enforcement with targeted policies to foster a safer and more empowering digital environment for children3. This approach strikes a careful balance between protection and empowerment, while fully respecting fundamental rights, including freedom of expression and communication. The Commission is not currently preparing an EU-wide ban, restriction, age limit, or mandatory identification requirement for virtual private network services. Regarding age verification, the Executive Vice-President for Technological Sovereignty, Security and Democracy, has emphasised the need for effective mechanisms to prevent minors from accessing harmful content online. In her statements, she highlighted the limitations of self-declaration systems, particularly in the context of pornographic platforms, where such measures have proven insufficient to shield children from age-inappropriate material. The Commission’s privacy preserving EU-wide age verification system is designed to address this challenge, ensuring that minors are better protected from exposure to harmful or inappropriate content while upholding data protection and privacy safeguards4.
1 https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/online-privacy. 2 Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 19 October 2022 on a Single

Market For Digital Services and amending Directive 2000/31/EC (Digital Services Act), OJ L 277, 27.10.2022, pp. 1–102. 3 https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/strategy-better-internet-kids. 4 https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/eu-age-verification.
